title: The LinksAI English law benchmark (Version 2)

author: Linklaters LLP

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The benchmark accepts the cluster’s core proposition and adds concrete English-law evidence for jagged, task-dependent capability: newer general-purpose models improve and can assist with familiar-law summaries or supervised drafting, but remain weaker on factual application and clause interpretation. Its recommendation for expert supervision, together with prompt- and context-sensitivity, strengthens the case for selective deployment, verification and use-specific evaluation rather than unsupervised reliance.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: LinksAI supports the cluster’s distinction between benchmark performance and dependable autonomous lawyering. It reports meaningful score improvements but persistent weakness in factual application and clause interpretation, and concludes that even positively marked outputs require expert supervision rather than direct reliance.
qs: In contrast, their ability to apply the law to the facts or interpret clauses is less good.
They do not constitute legal advice and should not be relied on even in situations where they have received a positive mark.

st.t: Legal benchmarks: Realistic tasks expose uneven competence
st.an: LinksAI supports the cluster’s proposition by evaluating a specific, practice-oriented task—English-law legal advice—and warning that superficially convincing outputs may still be incorrect or lack legal nuance and context. Its limited scope and absence of reported results mean it reinforces the cluster’s methodological and reliability claims without independently establishing uneven performance.
qs: The LinksAI English law benchmark has been created to test the capabilities of LLMs to deliver English law legal advice.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The benchmark supports the cluster’s core distinction between bounded technical capability and dependable legal autonomy. It finds general-purpose tools unreliable for critical-reasoning legal advice, stresses that real client needs require human translation into legal steps, and preserves a role for humans in legal-service delivery despite rapid model improvement. It does not materially address verification, training, organisational complements or apprenticeship risk.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: Linklaters supports realistic, task-specific evaluation by testing demanding English-law advice rather than relying on general impressions of fluency. Its findings that earlier answers were often wrong and contained fictional citations, while newer models may assist with first drafts, align with the cluster’s distinction between partial capability and dependable autonomous performance.

kp.k: Benchmark tests specialist English legal advice
kp.d: Linklaters tests 50 questions across 10 English-law practice areas, intended to resemble questions a competent specialist associate with 2 years post qualification experience could answer after research. Senior practice-area lawyers designed and marked the questions. The six models were general-purpose rather than specially trained for legal advice. Scores allocate 5 marks to substance, 3 to citations and 2 to clarity; a fictional citation attracts zero citation marks.
qs: The benchmark questions are relatively hard.
Substance (5 marks)
Citations (3 marks)
Clarity (2 marks)

kp.k: Newer models substantially improve benchmark scores
kp.d: The February 2025 report compares initial testing conducted in September 2023 with o1 and Gemini 2.0 testing conducted in December 2024. Overall scores out of 10 were GPT 2: 0.0, GPT 3: 3.3, GPT 4: 3.2, Bard: 4.4, Gemini 2.0: 6.0 and o1: 6.4. Gemini scored 2.7/5 for substance and 1.6/3 for citations; o1 scored 2.8/5 and 1.8/3 respectively. GPT 2's zero was presumptive, based on a small selection of questions, rather than an equivalent full assessment. The authors nevertheless judge the tested models below qualified-lawyer level.
qs: The LLMs we tested performed below the level of a qualified lawyer.
The best performer was OpenAI o1. It scored 6.4
GPT 3 and 4 were very similar

kp.k: Legal summarisation outperforms application and clause interpretation
kp.d: Across Gemini/o1 answers, 26% were mostly or fully accurate and complete, comparable to the authors' expectation of a competent researched 2-year PQE answer; 17% were entirely or almost entirely wrong. Just over half the questions involved summarising law, averaging 2.9/5 for substance, versus 2.6/5 for approximately 20 factual-application questions and 2.0/5 for three clause-interpretation questions. The authors acknowledge that more clause questions were needed for a fair result. Two additional clause questions scored Gemini 6 and 6, and o1 5 and 5, out of 10.
qs: The new models – The substance of the answers from Gemini 2.0 and OpenAI o1 was noticeably better.
On reflection we should have included more “clause” questions to get a fair result.

kp.k: Fabricated citations decline but remain a material risk
kp.d: The report finds fictional underlying case law or guidance in 47 of 150 answers from GPT 3, GPT 4 and Bard, described as a third of cases, compared with fictional citations in 9% of Gemini/o1 queries. These are findings from this benchmark, not universal model error rates. The Gemini example involving UBS AG v Rose Capital Ventures illustrates how an apparently plausible authority can have a nonexistent citation and fail to support the proposition advanced.
qs: We (still) need to talk about citations.
The problem is that this case does not exist.

kp.k: Confident presentation can conceal incorrect legal reasoning
kp.d: The authors describe both newer models as too eager to deliver a single definitive answer rather than explain uncertainty and alternative outcomes. Gemini sometimes included correct material alongside redundant or incorrect additions, while o1 was generally more concise. Their contrasting o1 examples show a 9/10 answer about Data Protection Act offences and an intellectual-property answer scoring 1/5 for substance, 0/3 for citations and 1/2 for clarity, which confused legal tests and omitted important issues.
qs: o1 achieved 9 out of 10 on this question.
But o1 does not always get the law right….
In contrast, o1 was generally short and to the point.

kp.k: Expert-supervised assistance remains the recommended deployment model
kp.d: Despite improvement, Linklaters recommends against using these models for English-law advice without expert human supervision. With that supervision, they may help produce first drafts or cross-check existing answers, particularly for well-known law. The report warns that errors and missing nuance make use dangerous when the user lacks a good idea of the answer. Positively marked benchmark answers are not legal advice and should not be relied upon.
qs: The latest models we tested may be useful but only when used
with expert human supervision.
They are still not always right

kp.d: An additional bonus-clause question tested whether models recognised multiple plausible interpretations of a drafting gap. The authors considered £0, £1000 and £2000 possible outcomes requiring discussion of interpretive uncertainty. A revised prompt requesting alternatives, reasoning and likelihoods improved Gemini's answer to 3/5 substance, 2/3 citations and 2/2 clarity, although the authors still criticised its legal reasoning. o1 retained the same definitive conclusion and received 2/5, 1/3 and 1/2. These limited experiments demonstrate model-specific responses, rather than a general measured benefit from prompt engineering.
qs: The right answer is “I don’t know”
OpenAI o1 didn’t perform that much better with a new prompt rubric
Gemini 2.0’s answer is much better with a new prompt rubric

kp.k: One-shot methodology trades interaction for repeatability
kp.d: Main benchmark questions used brief prompts and the first answer, without follow-up clarification or correction. Linklaters acknowledges that richer context, interaction and more sophisticated prompts could improve results, but defends its approach as standardised, repeatable and representative of less sophisticated users. Interactive testing could introduce inconsistent coaching, while detailed prompting adds work and can require prior knowledge of the answer.
qs: It might be possible to get better results from these LLMs by questioning them in an interactive fashion or using better prompts.
“One-shot”
Benchmarking constraints

kp.k: Human comparisons and practice-area rankings have limitations
kp.d: No actual 2-year PQE lawyers answered the benchmark: the authors cite difficulties controlling ability, available time, awareness of public testing and consultation with colleagues. Thus comparisons to junior-lawyer competence reflect expert marking expectations rather than a controlled human-model trial. Gemini/o1 averaged 7.0/10 in real estate and 3.9/10 in corporate, but question mix, difficulty and marking generosity may explain the difference. There was no central moderation. Repeated model queries could also produce different answers.
qs: No central moderation
I get a different answer
Why no “human in the loop”?

kp.k: Findings are jurisdiction-specific and do not establish RAG superiority
kp.d: The benchmark covers English-language questions on English or UK law. The authors speculate that US-law performance might be similar or better and performance on less common languages or legal systems worse, but neither proposition was tested here. They suggest specialist training or retrieval-augmented generation could improve results, while reporting that other models they tested were not significantly different from Gemini/o1; some results could not be published because permission was difficult to obtain.

kp.k: External studies broadly reinforce qualified reliability findings
kp.d: The report describes Allens' May 2024 Australian-law benchmark as finding GPT-4 strongest at 5.3/10, but even the best models inconsistently reliable and general tools unreliable on critical-reasoning tasks. It also reports that the May 2024 Stanford HAI legal-research study found specialised tools, including RAG tools, reduced but did not eliminate hallucinations, while noting disagreement with providers' tests. These are reported external findings, not results of LinksAI. The report also identifies other studies examining extraction, deployment and broader skills beyond legal advice.
qs: Our results are generally, but not always, consistent with other benchmarking exercises.
Allens AI Australian law benchmark
Stanford HAI AI on Trial (May 2024).

kp.k: Other legal workflows fall outside this benchmark
kp.d: Linklaters describes document summarisation, contract extraction, research and enhanced search, stylistic amendment and ideation as potential applications already accelerating legal service delivery. It also acknowledges contract drafting. The authors suggest these uses could significantly affect the sector, but explicitly do not evaluate these capabilities in this English-law advice benchmark.

kp.k: Future capability growth and lawyer displacement remain uncertain
kp.d: The authors treat continued rapid improvement as an open question: inherent limitations might cause a plateau, although they expect fine-tuning and training to improve performance for years. They do not endorse the quoted prediction that no jobs will be needed. Even eventual benchmark success would not necessarily remove lawyers, they argue, because clients often bring broad concerns or objectives rather than well-formed legal questions. Checking answers, applying them to circumstances and translating client objectives into legal steps remain distinct contributions.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Linklaters claims that newer general-purpose LLMs are becoming useful research assistants, but not reliable substitutes for expert English lawyers.
pts.d: In this February 2025 report, Linklaters says Gemini 2.0 and OpenAI o1 have improved sufficiently to approach usefulness for first drafts and cross-checking, provided expert human supervision is available. It reports better performance on summarising relatively familiar law than on applying law to facts or interpreting clauses, alongside continuing errors, fabricated citations and overconfident answers. Its preferred use is therefore lawyer augmentation rather than unsupervised advice. The report also says AI is already accelerating legal services through supporting tasks such as summarisation, extraction, research, stylistic revision and ideation, although these uses are outside this benchmark. More sophisticated prompts or interactive questioning may improve answers; its limited prompt experiments helped Gemini more than o1. Looking forward, Linklaters leaves open whether rapid progress will continue or plateau, while expecting further improvements from training and fine-tuning. It argues that even future benchmark success would not necessarily eliminate lawyers: checking applicability and translating broad business objectives into appropriate legal steps remain distinct from answering specified legal questions. These are Linklaters' conclusions, not an endorsement of the separately quoted Elon Musk prediction about jobs.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Linklaters' own expert-marked benchmark; broader productivity and professional-role claims are observations or arguments rather than measured outcomes.
pts.d: The benchmark uses 50 English-law questions across ten practice areas, intended to resemble research assignments for a competent specialist associate with two years' post-qualification experience. Senior practice-area lawyers marked substance out of five, citations out of three and clarity out of two. Reported overall scores were GPT 3: 3.3/10; GPT 4: 3.2/10; Bard: 4.4/10; Gemini 2.0: 6.0/10; and o1: 6.4/10. The model labelled GPT 2 was tested on a small selection and assigned a presumptive zero. For Gemini/o1, 26% of answers were mostly or fully accurate and complete, while 17% were entirely or almost entirely wrong; fictional citations occurred in 9% of queries, compared with 47 of 150 answers from GPT 3/4 and Bard. Their average substance scores varied by task: 2.9/5 for summarisation, 2.6/5 for factual application and 2.0/5 for clause interpretation. Only three original questions concerned clauses; two additional clause questions and alternative-prompt examples supplied limited further evidence. Examples include o1's relatively strong account of Data Protection Act offences and its weak price-index intellectual-property analysis. The report acknowledges no actual associate control group, answer variability, subjective marking, no central moderation and differences in question mix across practices. It references other studies as contextual corroboration, including Allens' Australian-law benchmark and Stanford's study of specialised legal research tools, while noting disagreement with provider tests. Its statements about sector-wide acceleration, future progress and lawyers' continuing role are not supported here by measured productivity, employment or market outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern models tested in September 2023 and December 2024, with supervised usefulness claimed as of February 2025 and future capability left uncertain.
pts.d: The report describes its first published exercise as October 2023 and its second as February 2025; the background section specifies actual testing in September 2023 and December 2024 respectively. Its advice-use conclusions are conditional on expert supervision and apply to the tested general-purpose models answering English-language English-law questions. The main exercise used short, standardised prompts and accepted the first answer without iterative correction; the rubric was similar but not identical between rounds. Linklaters accepts that richer context, interaction, specialist training or retrieval-augmented generation could improve results, but does not establish those improvements generally. It says other models it tested privately were not significantly different from Gemini 2.0 or o1, without publishing sufficient detail for a full comparison. It anticipates similar or better performance on US law and worse performance on less common languages or legal systems, explicitly treating these as outside scope rather than findings. Positively marked answers are not offered as legal advice or safe for reliance. Continued rapid improvement, a possible plateau and lawyers' longer-term role are conditional projections with no fixed displacement date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate implications concern English-law practitioners using AI and non-experts seeking advice, rather than a quantified restructuring of legal employment or markets.
pts.d: Specialist lawyers may gain drafting, research and cross-checking assistance but must retain responsibility for verification and nuanced application. Mid-level associates provide the benchmark's competence reference, not a measured category of displaced workers. Senior lawyers' supervision remains important because fluent output can conceal legal mistakes and fabricated authorities. Lay users and less sophisticated users face particular risks because they may neither recognise errors nor know what contextual information or follow-up questions are needed. Business clients typically bring broad concerns and objectives, which Linklaters argues require lawyers to identify the relevant questions and design legal steps rather than merely supply answers. Practice-area results differ—Gemini/o1 averaged 7.0/10 in real estate and 3.9/10 in corporate—but the report attributes possible differences to task mix, familiarity of subject matter, question difficulty and marking, rather than establishing unequal exposure to job substitution. It makes no quantified prediction about headcount, fees, staffing structures, firm market shares or access to justice.
